gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1052t:
VA and DOD Health Care, GAO-05-1052T of September 28, 2005, is an early look at how wounded troops move from Defense care to Veterans Affairs care. Since the Iraq and Afghanistan wars began, Defense counts more than 15,000 troops wounded in combat. The worst hurt need care from both systems in turn. A rough handoff can stall that care.

GAO lists the rules and outreach VA set up to greet new veterans fast. It then tests how much health data moves with each person in a set, tracked way. Rules and outreach earn praise. Data sharing stays thin, the title warns.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-322t:
Military Pay, GAO-05-322T of February 17, 2005, tells of hurt Guard and Reserve troops whose pay went wrong as they healed. Mass call-ups for the war on terror sent part-time troops to full war duty. Wounds and ills in the line of duty should keep pay and care in flow. In case after case, gaps cut both.

GAO asks if the Army's rules, steps, and tools could keep such pay true and on time. It finds flaws in all three fields. It asks if the Army's fresh fixes will last. The harm is plain: hurt troops faced debt and want while they could not work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-352t:
21st Century Challenges, GAO-05-352T of February 16, 2005, asks Congress to rethink the whole base of the federal state. A long-term cash gap grows as old vows outrun the tax take. The role and size of the state are in play. So is how to pay for the state that stays. Most perils here are slow, not sudden. They threat the life of kids and grandkids yet unborn.

The queries here grow out of GAO's years of work for Congress. They span cash, guard, health, and how the state runs. Few call for a fix this year. Each asks if a plan built for the last age still fits this one.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-382t:
Rural Housing Service, GAO-05-382T of March 10, 2005, asks if a farm housing aid arm built for the 1930s still fits the land of 2005. Roads, wires, and net links have tied much of farm land to the towns. Town sprawl eats the line that once split the two. Cash rules have grown tight in the same span. The aid arm lends and grants for homes in small towns and farm zones.

The facts here frame the arm's chief tests. Who counts as rural now shapes who can claim aid. Thin cash forces picks among loan, grant, and rent help. Past GAO work on who got in, and on shaky data, feeds the tale.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-392t:
United Nations, GAO-05-392T of March 2, 2005, warns that reform at the world body will fade with no steady watch. The U.N. core budget for 2004-2005 first topped $3 billion. Its chief launched reform waves in 1997 and 2002. GAO told of their state in February 2004. Probes of the Oil for Food plan have since bared old flaws in how the house is run.

The United States pays the largest share of that house. GAO lifts the fields where reform must bite, from aims to dead tasks. It rests on its 2004 tale and fresh Oil for Food work. Stay the watch, it urges.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-432t:
Proposed rules for the Defense Department's National Security Personnel System are reviewed in testimony GAO-05-432T, given on March 15, 2005. The new system would change how more than 700,000 defense civilian workers are hired, paid, promoted, and disciplined. The 2004 defense authorization act gave the department wide power to redesign those rules. Draft rules came out for public comment on February 14, 2005.

GAO said many ideas in the draft fit proven practice. These included pay bands, pay for performance, and weight given to performance in job cuts. But GAO raised three main concerns. The rules did not spell out how the system would run or what safeguards would guard against abuse. They did not require core skills that tell staff what their jobs demand. They also set no clear path for staff to stay involved. The testimony suggests a wider frame for reform across government.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-442t:
A further round of testimony on the Army's Future Combat Systems came in GAO-05-442T, presented on March 15, 2005. FCS aimed to field 18 linked manned and unmanned systems, from ground vehicles to sensors and munitions. The price tag for the first phase alone ran over $108 billion. GAO assessed the program's technical hurdles, its management load, and its chances of staying within budget.

The network at the heart of FCS had to move vast amounts of data in combat. Single vehicles were as complex as fighter aircraft. A lead systems integrator ran the program under a flexible deal called an Other Transaction Agreement. GAO warned that the Army would reach in 2008 the level of knowledge it should have held in 2003. With $4.6 billion already spent, only 1 of over 50 key technologies was mature. The testimony gives Congress a clear view of the risk.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-532t:
Oversight of the National Flood Insurance Program is the early topic of testimony GAO-05-532T, given on April 14, 2005. Flooding plays a part in 90 percent of U.S. natural disasters, and private insurers rarely cover it. Congress created the program in 1968 as an alternative to disaster aid. After Hurricane Isabel in September 2003, lawmakers heard complaints about coverage and claims. A 2004 law ordered GAO to study the program.

Policy limits and exclusions mean payouts may not cover full repair costs. Some limits sit in statute, and others the Federal Emergency Management Agency set. Officials said the limits keep premiums in line and the program sound. The work rests with thousands of agents and adjusters. About 40 agency staff, aided by about 170 contractor staff, watch over them. Four program managers told GAO agent knowledge varies widely. Training exists, but agents need not complete it. Flood adjusters, by contrast, face required training.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-542t:
Air traffic services run as businesses abroad are described in testimony GAO-05-542T, presented on April 20, 2005. By March 2005, 38 nations had shifted air navigation from government offices to independent providers. GAO studied five of them, in Australia, Canada, Germany, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom. It asked what traits they share, how safety and cost have fared, and what lessons stand out.

Each provider runs its own strategy, budget, and daily work. Each keeps safety as its first goal and answers to an outside safety regulator. All five say safety has held since the change. Data from Canada and New Zealand show fewer close calls between aircraft. Providers cut costs by merging sites and buying new technology. Fees fell for big airlines. Some small users, once subsidized, now pay more and fear future rises. The testimony offers a first look, with work still under way.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-572t:
Job help for disabled veterans is the charge of a VA program reviewed in testimony GAO-05-572T, given on April 20, 2005. The Vocational Rehabilitation and Employment program has grown in weight as troops come home hurt from Afghanistan and Iraq. GAO drew on 20 years of its work and on two recent reports. One judged a task force plan to remake the program. The other tracked help for the most seriously hurt.

GAO backed the task force's main verdicts. The program has not been a VA priority for getting disabled veterans back to work. It lacks the capacity to handle its growing load.  GAO also backed plans to simplify eligibility, expand counseling, and add staff. Three hurdles stand out. Recovery timing makes early help hard to plan. Defense officials fear VA outreach could hurt retention. VA also cannot get the Defense data needed to find every badly hurt servicemember.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-622t:
How block grant money reaches poor towns is weighed in GAO-05-622T, testimony of April 26, 2005. It reviews a housing department study of the Community Development Block Grant formula. GAO calls the study thoughtful and backs its yardstick of need. Two rival formulas split the money, so towns with like needs get unlike grants. Counting city size as need pulls funds toward bigger places.

A poverty count based on persons, not households, sends large grants to college towns. GAO airs fixes, from one formula to adding income per head. The study lands as the White House faults the program for missing high-need towns.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-662t:
Changes to veterans' job programs get early comment in GAO testimony GAO-05-662T, dated May 12, 2005. Two state-run services help the roughly 700,000 veterans out of work each month. A 2002 law split their roles: one serves disabled veterans directly, the other works with employers. States now set staffing, and 23 plan part-time outreach staff. Mixing the staffs into local job centers still proves awkward.

A common yardstick for states will not exist before 2007. The service met its 58 percent placement goal for all veterans in program year 2003 but fell short of 60 percent for disabled veterans. Oversight leans on state self-checks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-692t:
Why the securities watchdog missed mutual fund trading abuses is probed in GAO-05-692T, testimony of June 7, 2005. Before September 2003 the agency never examined funds for market timing or late trading. Staff ranked other risks higher and trusted firms to police themselves for profit's sake. New York's attorney general found the abuses first. GAO draws lessons: test controls directly, mine outside research, and guard the independence of fund compliance chiefs.

Since then the agency has added control checks, a risk office, and a rule for independent compliance officers. GAO says judging the cures will take time.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-722t:
Testimony GAO-05-722T, given on May 19, 2005, covers the move of badly hurt troops to veterans' care. More than 12,000 troops had been hurt in Iraq and Afghanistan. The Department of Veterans Affairs set up a task force to smooth the shift. GAO checked work to speed job training help for the badly hurt. It also checked the status of a data sharing deal.

GAO said the department gave these troops high priority but had trouble finding and tracking them. Both departments had agreed to share data in a set, routine way. The Defense Department raised privacy concerns, and no final deal was in place. GAO based its account on past work, talks with officials, and the health privacy law and rule.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-732t:
This testimony, GAO-05-732T (May 19, 2005), draws on four past GAO reports on the Endangered Species Act. The act guards more than 1,260 listed plants and animals. The Fish and Wildlife Service runs the act. All federal bodies must take care not to harm listed species or key habitat. GAO spoke to how agencies work together and how they use science.

GAO found that good teamwork can cut conflict over land use. At one base, the Air Force and wildlife staff lured an endangered pronghorn away from training grounds. That kept both training and the species safe. But GAO also found agencies could do more joint work. The wildlife service mostly used the best science at hand. Yet new research did not always feed into live choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-772t:
Private pension insurance is the warning topic of testimony GAO-05-772T, delivered June 9, 2005. A federal body insures the pensions of more than 34 million workers and retirees. Those workers sit in over 29,000 single-employer plans. In fiscal year 2004, the insurance program lost $12.1 billion. Its total deficit grew to $23.3 billion.

GAO said weak plan funding and weak rules drive the risk. The body faces almost $100 billion in underfunding at firms with poor credit ratings. Premiums do not match the risk each sponsor brings. Funding rules give sponsors weak reasons to fund their plans in full. Bankrupt sponsors have shifted large, short plans onto the insurer. GAO urged Congress to act sooner rather than later, and set out tests for reform.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-822t:
Early findings on hiring checks fill testimony GAO-05-822T, delivered June 21, 2005. A 1986 law set up the paper check employers run on new hires. It also set fines for breaches. Few changes have been made since. Experts say a more reliable check and stronger worksite enforcement are needed. GAO gave early views from its ongoing study.

GAO said fake documents and stolen identities have undermined the check. Employers who want to comply find it hard to hire only legal workers. Those who do not care find it easy to hire off the books. The wide range of accepted documents adds to the strain. A 1998 plan to cut that range was still not final. An electronic pilot shows promise to sharpen the check and aim enforcement better. Several challenges stand in its way, GAO added.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-842t:
Security clearance backlogs are updated in testimony GAO-05-842T, delivered June 28, 2005. The Defense Department holds about 2 million active clearances. It also clears staff for over 20 other bodies. Delays have plagued the system for over a decade. GAO put the program on its high-risk list in January 2005. In February 2005, the investigative arm moved to the personnel office.

GAO found some progress, with hurdles at each of the three stages. Naming which jobs need clearances is advancing for staff, but lags for contractors. Request handoffs between the two agencies snagged for 2 years. In February 2005, over 185,000 investigations had blown their time goals. Hiring more investigators helps, GAO said, but new staff may strain quality while they learn.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-892t:
Alien smuggling enforcement is graded in testimony GAO-05-892T, presented July 12, 2005. Smuggling earns billions of dollars a year worldwide. A new Homeland Security department opened a chance to attack smugglers' money. One arm handles investigations and financial crime skills. Another guards the border between entry points. In summer 2003, the investigations arm said a national strategy was coming. GAO drew on its May 2005 report.

As of July 5, 2005, the strategy was still not final. It was being refocused on the southwest border and all contraband. Lessons from an Arizona task force launched in October 2003 feed the draft. The two arms signed a deal in November 2004 on their roles. But no system tracks border referrals to investigators. That gap can let leads die, GAO noted. The federal response can be improved, it held.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-922t:
Extra federal oversight of Washington's transit body is weighed in testimony GAO-05-922T, presented July 28, 2005. The authority runs the region's subway and buses. It faces deep money strain, plus safety and reliability tests. Ridership sits at an all-time high. GAO set out the body's service to the federal government. It covered funding gaps, current overseers, and options if Congress adds aid.

GAO noted the system moves a large share of the federal workforce. Its police aid federal agencies and train first responders. Both regional and District emergency plans lean on it for evacuation. A regional panel put the funding shortfall at $2.4 billion for fiscal years 2006 through 2015. That count omits mandated disability transport costs, so the gap may run higher. GAO gave early views on safeguards for any new aid.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1012t:
Homeland Security buying gets a synthesis in testimony GAO-06-1012T, presented July 27, 2006. The department obligated almost $17.5 billion for goods and services in fiscal year 2005. Its needs run from airport screening gear to border tech. They include trailers for Katrina victims and upgrades to the Coast Guard fleet. GAO summed up its reports on this buying machine.

The testimony names areas where the department has fostered teamwork among its parts. It then lays out the challenges of uniting the buying function across so many components. A third part judges the review process for big, complex investments. The picture is of a young department with vast needs and a still-forming system. Readers get GAO's whole body of acquisition work in one account.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1022t:
Open records processing trends are analyzed in testimony GAO-06-1022T, delivered July 26, 2006. The Freedom of Information Act gives the public access to government records. Agencies report yearly to the Attorney General on their handling of requests. A recent executive order tells agencies to plan improvements, with goals to cut backlogs. GAO testified on the fiscal year 2005 reports and the new plans for 25 major agencies.

Headings from the ongoing work give the shape. Growth in requests is slowing, but pending cases keep rising. Most requests are granted in full. Processing times vary widely by agency. About half of the improvement plans lack goals for the backlog work the order demands. GAO said it expects to recommend steps when its review ends. The testimony stresses why the plans matter: without them, backlogs have no path down.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1032t:
Chemical review at the environmental agency is revisited in testimony GAO-06-1032T, given August 2, 2006. Chemicals fill daily life, from cleansers to plastics. Some, like lead and mercury, are highly toxic at set doses. A 1976 law lets the agency control chemicals that pose an unreasonable risk. The testimony rests on a June 2005 GAO report on the program.

That report described how the agency assesses chemicals in commerce. It covered controls on chemicals not yet in commerce. It also covered public disclosure of company data filed under the law. GAO urged Congress to consider giving the agency more authority to assess chemical risks. It urged the agency head to take several management steps. The agency did not disagree with the thrust of the report, the testimony notes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1092t:
World Trade Center responders and their long-term health are the center of GAO-06-1092T, testimony from September 2006. Rescue and cleanup crews faced many hazards, with lasting doubts about body and mind. In February 2006 GAO found four of five federal health programs had progressed. The federal responder screening program at the Department of Health and Human Services lagged. Congress had also given $75 million for monitoring and treatment. This statement updates both threads.

The screening program has since signed up more federal responders. An added 1,385 people brought the total to 1,762 by late August 2006. Plans formed to screen former federal workers outside the New York area. No one knows the full responder pool, so the share reached stays unknown. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had moved to award treatment funds, but plans were incomplete.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1112t:
Alternative mortgage products and the risks they hide are the subject of GAO-06-1112T, testimony given on September 20, 2006. These loans let borrowers defer principal, or even part of the interest, for the first years. Interest-only and payment-option loans grew fast as home prices climbed. GAO tracked market trends and the risks for borrowers and lenders. It also checked how well loan disclosures explain those risks, and how regulators responded.

GAO found the effect on defaults still unclear. Borrowers could face sharp payment shock when low early payments end. Lenders, in turn, face greater credit risk. Many borrowers seemed poorly informed about the terms they had signed. Mortgage ads and federal disclosure forms did not explain the risks clearly or fully. Federal banking regulators had issued guidance and sought industry and public comment. Most states in GAO's sample had also acted.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1122t:
Federal climate change spending reports are critiqued in GAO-06-1122T, testimony presented on September 21, 2006. Congress requires yearly reports on this funding. The Office of Management and Budget reports sums for technology, science, aid abroad, and tax breaks. A science program office also reports on research funding. GAO's statement draws on its August 2005 report and covers funding from 1993 through 2004.

GAO found that the reports changed form over time, so year-to-year comparisons often failed. Totals by category and by agency could not always be tracked on a steady basis. GAO urged OMB and the science office to keep one format, explain any changes, and supply a crosswalk when formats shift. It also urged OMB to add data on climate tax breaks. Finally, it asked OMB to seek clear direction from Congress on which budget figures to report.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-142t:
A draft law to remake federal personnel rules gets early comment in GAO-06-142T, testimony from October 2005. The proposed Working for America Act would make federal pay more market based and tied to performance. The Office of Personnel Management would design a new job classification and pay system. GAO shared early views and the principles it thinks reform must meet.

GAO backs market-based, performance-oriented pay as both doable and wise. Reform, though, cannot sit on top of weak performance systems. Agencies need sound management basics and real resources first. GAO urged a phased path with a show-me test for each agency. The personnel office would certify that an agency's groundwork meets set standards. GAO advised Congress to move first on pay reform. It urged more caution on labor relations and appeals changes, where experience is thin.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-182t:
Theft of explosives from government storage sites is examined in GAO-06-182T, testimony dated October 31, 2005. Americans use over 5.5 billion pounds of explosives each year. The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives licenses private storage sites. A July 2004 theft of several hundred pounds from a local government site raised alarm. GAO counted thefts from state and local sites, mapped the bureau's powers, and checked security at sites it visited.

Agency data show few such thefts: 9 reports from January 2002 to February 2005, against 205 thefts from all sources. GAO itself found 5 thefts, one missing from the national database. The true count may run higher. The bureau has no power to inspect state and local sites, since they need no license. It does not even track how many such sites exist. The 18 sites GAO visited used gates, fences, patrols, and routine counts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-242t:
Fifteen years of federal financial reform are marked in GAO-06-242T, testimony presented on November 17, 2005. The Chief Financial Officers Act of 1990 was the broadest money reform law in 40 years. Before it, tales of fraud and waste painted a government that could not guard its own funds. The act set a leadership structure for agency finance. It ordered yearly audited statements and modern systems with strong controls.

The testimony traces the act's roots and its main parts. It grades how far agencies have come in living up to it. It then names the challenges that lie ahead. Clean audits are now the norm at big agencies, a sharp break with the past. Useful cost data for daily choices still lag. The statement frames the act as a long drive, not a single fix. Its lessons guide the next round of reform.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-322t:
The legal frame around New Orleans' levees is mapped in GAO-06-322T, testimony presented December 15, 2005. Storm surge from hurricanes is the region's gravest natural threat. In 1965 Congress told the Army Corps of Engineers to build a levee system for the area. The federal side paid 70 percent of costs; state and local sponsors paid 30. The Corps designed and built the levees. GAO was asked to explain the rules that govern them.

The statement lays out five points. It states the protection level Congress set. It assigns who must operate, maintain, and repair the levees. It covers who acts when levees fail. It reviews the Corps' plans for emergency response. GAO made no recommendations at this stage. After Katrina, this dry framework reads as the fine print of a catastrophe. Knowing who owned which duty is the first step to fixing it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-412t:
Drivers faced soaring pump prices, and oil firms posted large profits. Testimony GAO-06-412T, given February 1, 2006, explains factors behind higher gasoline prices. Each extra ten cents per gallon adds about $14 billion to the nation's yearly gasoline bill. That figure comes from the Energy Information Administration. Heavy use of motor vehicles makes the cost hit wide.

GAO asks what drives gasoline prices. It traces the pattern of oil company mergers in recent years. It then weighs merger effects on market concentration and wholesale prices. The testimony draws on three earlier GAO works and updated data. Readers get market causes, not just price spikes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-442t:
One of the largest disasters in U.S. history strained every level of government. GAO decided to present GAO-06-442T on March 8, 2006: early views on Hurricane Katrina. Hurricane Rita soon added to the load in the same region. Back-to-back catastrophes showed how response systems can be overwhelmed. GAO had a large body of work under way on the storms.

The testimony covers preparation before the storm. It covers response once Katrina hit. It also covers early recovery. GAO labels the observations preliminary. That timing matters, since much work was still going on. Readers get an early map of failure points. Later reports would test these first views.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-462t:
Investigators at an immigration agency must be placed where they do the most good. Testimony GAO-06-462T, given March 28, 2006, covers Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Its Office of Investigations probes customs and immigration violations. The office supports a mission to prevent terrorist attacks in the United States. It must still carry out its customs, immigration, and protective duties.

GAO describes the structure and activities the office adopted. It tracks how the office used investigative resources in fiscal year 2004 and half of fiscal year 2005. It asks how resource use guards weak points in customs and immigration systems. Better management practices could help, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-482t:
A law meant to expose bad payments entered its second year of government-wide reports. Testimony GAO-06-482T, dated March 9, 2006, reviews the Improper Payments Information Act of 2002. Fiscal year 2005 was the second year agencies had to report under the act. Agencies must find programs at risk of improper payments. They must estimate amounts and report steps to cut them. Those reports go in yearly performance and accountability reports.

GAO reports progress in meeting the act's demands. It looked at risk assessments and yearly estimates. It also tracked sums recovered through recovery audits. Challenges remain, GAO said. Readers get the scale of improper payments and the state of agency work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-492t:
Firms selling to the government while owing taxes are the focus here. Delivered March 14, 2006, testimony GAO-06-492T covers General Services Administration contractors and unpaid federal taxes. The agency arranges billions in goods and services through schedules and other contracts. Earlier GAO testimony in February 2004 and June 2005 found contractor tax abuse elsewhere. That record raised concern about schedule contractors.

GAO was asked whether such contractors owe federal taxes. It measured the size of any debts. It gave examples tied to abusive or criminal activity. It also checked whether the agency screens for tax debts before awards. The title states the scale plainly: thousands abused the tax system.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-532t:
Fair play in the livestock market depends on probes that finish and bite. In testimony GAO-06-532T (March 9, 2006), GAO reviews the Packers and Stockyards programs. The Grain Inspection, Packers and Stockyards Administration enforces the act. The livestock market is worth $90 billion. Past reports by GAO and the Agriculture inspector general found flaws in investigations. A newer inspector general report shows key advice still unmet.

GAO draws on its prior work for this statement. It names factors that limit probes of anticompetitive practice. It tracks actions taken on its recommendations and where efforts fell short. Problems continue, GAO said. Readers get the enforcement record and the challenges ahead.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-542t:
Visa officers stand on the front line, and waits at consulates had grown long. On April 4, 2006, testimony GAO-06-542T covered consular resources and visa delays. After the September 11 attacks, new border security steps added to consular workload. Officers must block those who would harm U.S. interests. They must also speed legitimate travel. GAO had issued a series of reports on the visa process in recent years.

This statement discusses wait times for visas. It names factors that affect those waits. It sums up GAO work on consular staffing. A fresh look at resource needs could help address delays, GAO said. Readers get the security and service balance.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-562t:
Airport grants and air traffic upgrades rest on one trust fund's health. Delivered March 28, 2006, testimony GAO-06-562T analyzes the Airport and Airway Trust Fund. The fund was set up by a 1970 law. It pays for all of the Federal Aviation Administration's capital accounts. Those include airport grants, facilities and equipment, and research. At times it has also paid part of agency operations. The fund received $10.8 billion in fiscal year 2005.

The taxes feeding the fund expire at the end of fiscal year 2007. GAO was asked for analysis of the fund's condition and future viability. Readers get revenue sources and the stakes of expiry.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-572t:
The fund that pays for highways could go negative within a few years. GAO's GAO-06-572T testimony, delivered April 4, 2006, gives an overview of Highway Trust Fund estimates. The fund is fed by excise taxes on highway users, such as fuel taxes. The Treasury and the Congressional Budget Office each estimate future receipts twice a year. Their latest estimates show the Highway Account could have a negative balance as early as 2009. A new highway law had just been authorized on the promise of those funds.

Congress asked GAO to compare the two sets of estimates. GAO also compares past estimates with actual receipts. Readers get how the balance forecast is built.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-602t:
Turning 55 million gallons of radioactive waste into a stable form is a massive build. Testimony GAO-06-602T, dated April 6, 2006, covers the Hanford Waste Treatment Plant. The plant sits at the Energy Department's Hanford site in southeastern Washington. In 2000, the department gave Bechtel National an 11-year, $4.3 billion contract to design and build it. Since then, many problems and changes have raised cost and pushed the finish date. The testimony rests on past GAO reports and ongoing work.

GAO explains how and why cost and schedule changed since 2000. It reports efforts by the department and contractor to fix management. Contractor and department problems drove the trouble, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-622t:
Federal contracts for Hurricane Katrina recovery are the topic of GAO-06-622T, testimony presented on April 10, 2006. Storms Katrina and Rita had devastated the Gulf Coast months earlier. The federal reply leaned heavily on private contractors to house victims, clear debris, and restore services. At the same time, buying staffs at several agencies were already on GAO's high-risk list.

GAO told the Senate panel that many recovery contracts were awarded in great haste, with weak planning. Cost controls and oversight often lagged behind the urgent work. GAO drew lessons from past disasters about how to plan contracts before a crisis hits. The testimony explains why contract management can make or break a disaster response.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-632t:
Training that helps other nations block terrorist money is the subject of GAO testimony GAO-06-632T, dated April 6, 2006. Cutting off funds is meant to stop terrorists from organizing, recruiting, and equipping followers. A working group led by the Department of State coordinates this training for priority nations seen as most at risk. Other vulnerable nations also receive help.

GAO found that the United States lacked one integrated strategy to guide this work. Key agencies disagreed about roles and procedures. GAO said the effort did not match resources well to the level of risk in each nation. The government also lacked a clear record of the budget spent on this training. GAO urged tighter planning and coordination across agencies.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-702t:
Science and math degrees are tracked in GAO-06-702T, testimony presented on May 3, 2006. The United States leads the world in science and technology innovation. The federal government spends billions on education in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics, called STEM fields. Yet doubts persist about whether the nation can keep its edge. GAO charted degree trends over a decade and the role of federal programs.

GAO found that total college enrollment rose, but the STEM share of degrees fell. About 519,000 students earned STEM degrees in academic year 1994-1995, some 32 percent of all degrees. By academic year 2003-2004, about 578,000 earned them, yet the share dropped to 27 percent. The testimony weighs what federal programs can and cannot do about the trend.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-742t:
Energy futures markets and how GAO planned to study them are laid out in GAO-06-742T, testimony presented on May 4, 2006. Crude oil and natural gas prices had hit record highs. Many in Congress and the public suspected that forces beyond supply and demand were at work. GAO described its ongoing study of how futures markets and their players shape prices. Producers and refiners use futures to manage price risk, and new kinds of investors had entered since 2000.

The testimony explains the approach GAO would take to examine federal oversight of these markets. It sets out the questions on trading, speculation, and price formation that the study would test. Rather than give final answers, the statement frames the inquiry. Readers learn what evidence GAO meant to gather and why energy price swings drew scrutiny.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-822t:
Planning for the 2010 Census is warned over in GAO-06-822T, testimony presented on June 6, 2006. The census is required by the Constitution and runs on fixed deadlines. Its data steer about $200 billion a year in federal aid and reapportion House seats. The Census Bureau estimated the 2010 count would cost $11.3 billion. It planned to reengineer the paper-based methods used in past counts, adding handheld technology and a short-form-only design.

GAO called the census an expensive but vital undertaking. GAO urged that costs and risks be closely watched and judged as the decade advances. Mitigation plans, GAO said, must be in place before problems grow. The bureau's redesign promised savings and accuracy gains, but it also carried delivery risks. The testimony sets the oversight tone for the count.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-892t:
Federal courthouse rent, now over $900 million a year paid by the courts to the General Services Administration, is the subject of GAO testimony GAO-06-892T, dated June 22, 2006. In December 2004 the courts sought a $483 million yearly rent break. The agency refused it.

GAO traced recent trends in court rent and space. New space, plus rising energy and security costs, drove the growth. GAO also weighed how well the courts track and manage those costs. It urged the courts to track rent trends and reward lean use of space. The testimony lays out a cost fight inside the federal estate.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-992t:
Health gains from clean air rules are the focus of GAO testimony GAO-06-992T, dated July 19, 2006. Fine particles in air are linked to asthma and early death. The Environmental Protection Agency sets national air norms for such particles, and weighs the costs and gains of each change.

In January 2006 the agency put forth revised norms, with a study of their effects. A 2002 National Academies report had told the agency how to make health gain estimates better. GAO checked how far the agency used that advice in the 2006 study. It rests on GAO report GAO-06-780, issued the same month. More progress is needed, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1002t:
Working from home in federal jobs needs a sharper focus on results, GAO states in testimony GAO-07-1002T, dated June 12, 2007. Telework can keep work going in a crisis. It can also cut energy use and pollution.

The statement pulls from past GAO work on federal telework. It lists key steps for sound telework plans, drawn from a 2003 report. It adds a 2005 study of how five agencies define and gauge telework. It closes with GAO views on a 2007 Senate bill, S. 1000, to boost telework. Readers get a brief guide to what makes telework more than a perk.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1022t:
Drug plan sign-up for people on both Medicare and Medicaid is described in GAO testimony GAO-07-1022T, dated June 21, 2007. A 2003 law moved drug cover for these dual-eligible people to Medicare Part D. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services must place them in a drug plan if they pick none.

The agency placed about 5.5 million such people in late 2005. It placed about 634,000 more who qualified during 2006. GAO told how new sign-ups work, and how the process affects access to drugs. It set out how the agency set the start date of cover. The testimony rests on GAO report GAO-07-272.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1042t:
New chemical risks at defense sites are summed up in GAO testimony GAO-07-1042T, dated July 12, 2007. Two stand out. Trichloroethylene, a metal cleaner used widely by the Defense Department, can harm health. Perchlorate, used in missiles and rockets, turns up in water and soil across the country.

Such chemicals lack set norms, or their norms are in flux. GAO drew on past work to state what is known of each risk. It set out the department's duties for taint at its sites. It listed what the department has done so far. Perchlorate poses a marked risk to unborn children, the work notes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1122t:
Claimed gains from an aid deal with Vanuatu are overstated, GAO states in testimony GAO-07-1122T, dated July 26, 2007. The Millennium Challenge Corporation signed a 5-year, $65.7 million deal with the island nation. It said the deal would change the economy, raise income, and aid 65,000 poor rural people.

The testimony sums up GAO's July 2007 report, GAO-07-909. GAO checked how the body projects gains from its deals. It weighed how it states and tests those gains for Vanuatu. It named risks that could blunt the deal's effect. GAO urged clearer public claims, a check of other deals, and fuller weight for risk.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1132t:
A diverse workforce and strong outreach can aid the 2010 Census, GAO states in testimony GAO-07-1132T, dated July 26, 2007. The Census Bureau must count a nation that grows larger, more mixed, harder to find, and less keen to take part. It must do so at a fair cost.

The testimony rests mainly on past GAO work. It gives facts on diversity in the bureau's own workforce. It sets out plans to partner with local groups, to build public notice of the count. It covers rules that guard contract chances for small firms. The count's fate, GAO argues, rests in part on trust built street by street.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1142t:
Disaster readiness at the Homeland Security Department and its emergency agency is summed up in GAO testimony GAO-07-1142T, dated July 31, 2007. The Federal Emergency Management Agency faces a new season while it reshapes under a 2006 reform law. The law aimed to firm up its work before and after great disasters.

GAO has reported lasting hurdles: clear lines of lead, the skills a reply needs, and systems that guard aid from waste and fraud. The short statement sums up findings on those hurdles. It tells what both bodies have done on them. It closes with disaster points that still call for congressional watch.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1152t:
Americans at U.N. agencies are again too few, GAO states in testimony GAO-07-1152T, dated August 1, 2007. The United States is the largest funder of most U.N. bodies. The State Department says Americans bring skills and values that lift those bodies' work.

The testimony rests on a GAO report dated September 6, 2006. GAO set out U.S. staff share and trends at five U.N. organizations. It named what helps or blocks them in meeting U.S. hiring aims. It weighed State Department efforts to lift the share. Stronger efforts are needed, the title states, and the statement lists more that can be done.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1222t:
How should Congress track whether Iraq is meeting its pledges? GAO's answer came in testimony GAO-07-1222T, issued September 5, 2007. The statement reports GAO's check of 18 legislative, security, and economic benchmarks. A 2007 act set those benchmarks and required this report. GAO also used a partly met rating where progress fell short of full success.

GAO found that Iraq's government had met only 3 of the 18 benchmarks. Four more were partly met, and 11 were not met at all. Promised laws from June 2006 on reconciliation had not been fulfilled. GAO focused its advice on the quality of reporting to the President. It asked State to spell out where each Iraqi law stands. It asked Defense to give fuller data on violence and on Iraqi force readiness.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-252t:
Fraud in hurricane relief aid kept surfacing long after the storms passed. GAO laid out fresh cases in testimony GAO-07-252T on December 6, 2006. The relief agency's housing program paid rent help to storm victims. GAO mined agency records for double payments. It also traced relief gear bought with government purchase cards. Field teams checked sites in Louisiana and Texas.

Some victims took rent money while living free in agency trailers, GAO found. The agency paid nearly $20 million twice to people claiming damage from both storms. Fifty payments worth almost $156,000 went to 25 workers barred from the program by visa status. GAO's earlier $1 billion fraud estimate now looks low, the testimony says. Purchase card controls were also weak. Of 246 laptops, printers, boats, and GPS units checked, 85 were missing. GAO had already sent 25 fixes to the agencies.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-262t:
Families can get college help from grants, loans, or the tax code, and the mix confuses many. GAO summed up the tangle in testimony GAO-07-262T on December 5, 2006. The statement updates GAO's 2005 report on education aid. It compares student aid programs with tax breaks. It asks how well filers use the breaks. It also asks what proof exists that aid changes choices.

Many filers leave money unclaimed, GAO found. About 374,000 filers who seemed eligible claimed no education tax break. They lost $169 each on average. Roughly 447,000 more picked a break that saved them less than another would. Half of those weak choices sat on returns by paid preparers. In undercover visits, preparers also stumbled on the rules. Little solid evidence shows whether aid raises attendance, GAO said. It urged a simpler, better-tested aid strategy.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-342t:
The nation's long-term budget path is unsustainable, the Comptroller General told senators. The warning came in testimony GAO-07-342T on January 11, 2007. The Senate Budget Committee heard the statement. It lays out five points about the fiscal future. Staying on the current path would erode the economy, living standards, and security, the testimony says. The statement draws on GAO's long-running fiscal simulations.

First, the current fiscal condition is worse than advertised. Second, the long-term outlook is imprudent and cannot hold. Third, better information and budget processes can help. Fourth, fixing the path demands tough choices. It will take bipartisan cooperation and compromise. Fifth, the time to act is now, not later. Delay raises the cost of every fix. The testimony urges leaders to face the trade-offs openly.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-422t: Food stamp errors were falling in 2007, and GAO's briefing says payment mistakes and trafficking had declined even as enrollment grew. The testimony credits the progress. The findings show the safety net was getting tighter. The hunger program was learning to count.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-442t: Passenger trains were soft targets in 2007, and GAO's briefing says a federal strategy with better coordination was needed to guide security. The testimony demands the plan. The findings warn that the rails carried millions with too little guarding. The rails deserved a real shield.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-452t: The security mega-agency's to-do list was daunting in 2007, and GAO's briefing lays out the management and program hurdles. The testimony is a frank inventory. The findings warn that bigness is not the same as readiness. The size was not the same as the strength.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-502t: The land agency's house was a mess in 2007, and GAO's briefing lays out the big troubles facing the bureau. The briefing lists the failures for Congress. The findings warn that the nation's landlord was shirking its own upkeep. The public lands deserved better care.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-512t: Disabled veterans' claims were stuck in the queue in 2007, and GAO's briefing says the long-standing processing troubles persisted. The testimony measures the backlog in detail. The findings' plea is moral: the wounded should not wait years for what they earned.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-532t: The VA's computers were still full of holes in 2007, and GAO's briefing says the department had to address its long-standing weaknesses. The testimony repeats the charge. The findings warn that veterans' private data deserved better locks. The veterans' data deserved better than this.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-542t: The nation's fiscal stewardship was failing in 2007, and GAO's briefing names the critical accountability challenges facing America. The testimony sounds the alarm. The findings warn that the country's money management was living on borrowed time. The red ink was not waiting for permission.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-562t: Disabled veterans waited too long for their benefits in 2007, and GAO's briefing says the claims backlog kept presenting challenges. The testimony measures the delays. The findings' plea is moral: those who served should not have to fight the paperwork too.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-582t: Iraq's forces could not keep themselves supplied in 2007, and GAO's briefing offers early observations on their logistics gaps. The testimony previews the shortfalls in detail. The findings warn that the army America was building could not feed or fuel itself.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-612t: Building Iraq's army was harder than planned in 2007, and GAO's briefing names the factors blocking capable Iraqi security forces. The testimony lists the impediments one by one. The findings warn that the handoff of the war kept slipping further away.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-632t: The visitor-tracking system was stumbling in 2007, and GAO's briefing says the US-VISIT program faced operational, tech, and management woes. The testimony lists the troubles in full detail. The findings warn that the border's digital eye badly needed glasses.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-672t: The Army's future fighting machines were a risk pile in 2007 — GAO's briefing says the Future Combat System's dangers showed why oversight mattered. The testimony sounds the alarm. The findings warn that the tank of tomorrow could not be bought on promises.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-682t: The oil-royalty collectors were still fumbling in 2007 — GAO's briefing says Interior's efforts to get taxpayers a fair return needed real fixing. The testimony repeats the charge with force. The findings' refrain: the public's oil should pay the public's price.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-742t: Federal contractors were stiffing the taxman in 2007 — GAO's briefing says thousands of firms that owed taxes still won government work. The testimony exposes the double standard in detail. The findings ask why the government paid tax cheats to do its jobs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-812t: Transit-building grants were under the microscope in 2007 — GAO's briefing offers an early read on the New Starts and Small Starts programs. The testimony tracks the rule changes and trends. The findings ask whether the rail-money pipeline was flowing to the worthiest tracks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-822t: Homeland Security's info-sharing web needed weaving in 2007 — GAO's briefing says the department's network had to mesh better with state and local partners. The testimony demands real coordination. The findings' point is sharp: a network nobody joins is just a wire.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-832t: The Pentagon bought services like confetti in 2007 — GAO's briefing says managing those deals needed a serious upgrade, and soon. The testimony targets the oversight gap in full detail. The findings warn that services spending had become the budget's fastest-growing blind spot.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-842t: Security clearances for contractors moved at a crawl in 2007 — GAO's briefing finds long waits and thin files for industry workers needing access. The testimony exposes the vetting backlog in plain terms. The findings warn that the line to guard the secrets was itself becoming a weak link.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-852t: Wounded troops' charts were still not traveling with them in 2007 — GAO's briefing says the VA and Pentagon shared more data but stayed far from one record. The testimony's frustration shows. The findings demand the chart follow the patient, at last.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-862t: Telling doctors how they practiced could cut waste in 2007 — GAO's briefing says systematic feedback on practice patterns was a promising lever. The testimony makes the case for data-driven medicine. The findings bet that sunlight on habits will change the habits.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-872t: The watchdog turned the lens inward in 2007 — GAO's briefing reports on its own people-transformation drive. The testimony grades the auditor's HR overhaul with unusual candor. The findings show the accountability shop holding itself to the same account it demands of others.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-922t: Wildfire bills were exploding in 2007 — GAO's briefing says better management could help federal agencies hold down the cost of the burn. The testimony pairs fire science with budget sense. The findings argue that smart thinning and planning beat writing blank checks to the flames.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1032t: GAO shared its findings on nuclear Weapons: Views on NNSA's Proposal to Transform the Nuclear Weapons Complex with Congress in 2008. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-132t: GAO urged Congress in 2007 to give the Pentagon a full-time fix-it boss with a locked-in term — a chief manager who could outlast the revolving door of brass. Reform drives kept dying with each changing of the guard. The briefing's pitch: only a term-safe leader could drag lasting change through the world's biggest bureaucracy.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-142t: GAO told Congress in 2007 that Homeland Security had handed too much core work to hired firms with too little watching. Billions in safety work flowed to contractors while the agency's grip stayed loose. The briefing argues the department must sort what only feds should do — then keep a hard eye on the rest.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-192t: GAO told Congress in 2007 that checks on arriving travelers still had holes, despite recent gains. Secret probes at airports and land ports found staff missing red flags they should have caught. The briefing argues the front door of the nation needs a tighter lock — and sketches what it would take to get border screening right.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-212t: GAO told Congress in 2007 why no joint plan existed to bring the web back after a knockout blow. The net's pipes are privately owned, but a nationwide blackout would be everyone's crisis — and neither side had mapped the rescue. The briefing digs into the trust gaps and turf lines that kept government and tech firms from planning the fix together.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-222t: This 2007 Government Accountability Office testimony tackles a quiet drain on retirement savings: the fees buried inside 401(k) plans. GAO argues that employers sponsoring plans and workers saving in them need clearer information to understand what fees they are paying and how those fees compound. The report makes the case that opacity in retirement-plan pricing costs ordinary savers real money.
